title: Comments That Merely Narrate the Code
pattern: A comment translates the adjacent identifiers or operations into prose without contributing intent, context, or otherwise non-obvious information.
why_bad: Redundant prose obscures the executable logic, adds maintenance and alignment work, and can drift into misleading descriptions after code changes.
detection: Compare comment content with nearby active code. Include a single redundant preceding comment whose prose matches the identifiers or operator semantics of the adjacent line; a trailing `//` comment on the same line as a statement that only restates it; and a run of three or more consecutive statements or blocks each immediately preceded by a single-line comment translating the code. Placement or comment density alone is not enough when the text adds information.
counterexample: Comments explaining a subtle domain-specific invariant, a hardware-level quirk, or other intent not apparent from the code alone; short endline annotations carrying non-obvious data such as units or protocol field names on packed struct fields; and statements grouped into logical paragraphs with blank lines and at most one intent comment per paragraph.
fix: Delete only the redundant narration. For long narrated runs, organize statements with blank lines into paragraphs of logical intent, retaining useful intent or invariant comments.
source: Kent Beck, *Tidy First* (2023), Chapter 15 ("Delete Redundant Comments"), pp. 29-31; Robert C. Martin, *Clean Code* (2008), Chapter 4, p. 61; Steve McConnell, *Code Complete* (2004), Chapter 32 ("Endline Comments and Their Problems"); Steve McConnell, *Code Complete* (2004), Chapter 32.2 ("Optimum Number of Comments"); John K. Ousterhout, *A Philosophy of Software Design* (2018), Chapter 13.2 ("Red Flag: Comment Repeats Code").
